content: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) is a relatively rare condition but represents one of the most common hip disorders in children and adolescents. It is characterized by instability of the growth plate (physis) located at the junction of the femoral head and neck. This instability results in the femoral head remaining in the acetabulum while the femoral neck slips forward and outward. Although the exact cause of SUFE is not well understood, several anatomical and medical factors have been implicated. These include increased body weight (above the 80th percentile), femoral retroversion (greater than 10 degrees), increased height of the physis due to a widened hypertrophic zone, a more vertical orientation of the physis, and trauma. Additionally, certain medical conditions such as endocrine disorders, renal osteodystrophy, and prior radiation therapy are associated with an increased risk of SUFE. Approximately 30% of patients with SUFE develop bilateral involvement, with the contralateral hip slipping as well. The incidence of SUFE is estimated at 10 per 100,000 children, though this may be an underestimation as mild cases may go undiagnosed until arthritis develops later in life. SUFE is more common in boys, accounting for 75% of cases, with peak incidence occurring between 12 and 15 years of age. In girls, the peak incidence is slightly earlier, between 10 and 13 years. SUFE is rarely reported after the age of 20. The typical presentation of SUFE involves an overweight child who complains of groin, thigh, or knee pain, often accompanied by a limp. The pain may be referred via the obturator nerve. There may be a history of minor trauma. Depending on the severity, the child may be able to walk (stable slip) or may be unable to ambulate even with crutches (unstable slip). In cases where the child can walk, external rotation of the affected limb is often observed, and the child may be unable to sit comfortably without keeping the leg straight due to restricted hip flexion. As the severity of the condition increases, pain and disability also worsen. SUFE can be classified based on weight-bearing status. A stable slip allows the patient to ambulate and bear weight, while an unstable slip does not. In a study of 55 cases, avascular necrosis (AVN) was observed in 47% of unstable slips but in none of the stable slips. Anatomical reduction of the slip was achieved in 26 of 30 unstable cases but only in 2 of 25 stable cases. AVN is a serious complication of SUFE, characterized by the death of bone tissue due to loss of blood supply. Another potential complication is chondrolysis, which involves the gradual thinning and loss of articular cartilage. Chronologically, SUFE can be classified into four categories: preslip, acute, chronic, and acute-on-chronic. Preslip refers to cases where symptoms are present but there is no anatomical displacement of the femoral head, though radiological signs such as widening of the physis may be evident. Acute SUFE involves abrupt displacement of the proximal physis with symptoms developing over less than three weeks. Chronic SUFE presents with pain in the groin, thigh, or knee that may persist for months or years. Acute-on-chronic SUFE occurs when a patient with chronic symptoms experiences a sudden increase in the degree of slip. Radiographic classification of SUFE is based on the degree of displacement, either as a proportion of the femoral neck width or by angular displacement. Mild slips (Grade I) involve less than one-third displacement, moderate slips (Grade II) involve one-third to one-half displacement, and severe slips (Grade III) involve more than one-half displacement. Angular displacement is measured using the Southwick angle, with mild slips defined as less than 30 degrees, moderate slips as 30 to 50 degrees, and severe slips as greater than 50 degrees. The treatment of SUFE is primarily surgical, with the goal of preventing further slippage while minimizing complications such as AVN and chondrolysis. For Grade I and some Grade II slips, the standard treatment involves percutaneous pinning in situ (PIS), where a single screw is placed across the growth plate through a small incision. In some cases, multiple smooth pins may be used, particularly in very young children under the age of 8, to allow for continued growth. The screw should not be removed before physeal closure to prevent further slippage. For more severe slips, corrective surgery or reduction may be necessary. However, forceful closed reduction is contraindicated due to the high risk of AVN. Open reduction and fixation may be performed using techniques such as Dunn’s osteotomy, Fish osteotomy, or surgical dislocation, though the relative effectiveness of these methods remains debated. The timing of surgery for unstable SUFE is controversial. Some studies suggest that early stabilization within 24 hours may reduce the risk of AVN, while others have not found a statistically significant difference. Prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip is also debated, as the risk of a contralateral slip varies widely (18–60%). Factors influencing the decision to perform prophylactic pinning include the child’s age (younger children are at higher risk), the underlying cause of the slip (e.g., renal osteodystrophy or endocrine disorders), and the severity and nature of the current slip. The ultimate goal of SUFE treatment is to provide mechanical stability to prevent further slippage while avoiding complications such as AVN and chondrolysis. Long-term outcomes may include residual displacement, which can impair function and quality of life. In such cases, realignment procedures such as trochanteric, subtrochanteric, or femoral neck osteotomy may be performed. In older patients with degenerative changes, total hip replacement may be necessary. Reducing the slip can improve stability and function while potentially preventing long-term complications, provided short-term complications are avoided. The management of SUFE remains a topic of ongoing debate and evolution, influenced by advancements in surgical techniques and understanding of the condition. The rarity of SUFE, combined with the lack of robust evidence and standardized treatment guidelines, has led to significant variability in clinical practice. This variability underscores the need for rigorous, evidence-based recommendations to optimize care for patients with SUFE.
